Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight that he must speak with me, and I knew at once what such a message meant, as such messages generally do.

We met the next day at a coffee house in the town, where he was already seated, and so busy over the instrument in his hand that he did not at first perceive me. He looked nervous, and in the same breath professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his own.

I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded and said that it was all right, and then walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

My friend was of opinion that I made too much of the business; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me notwithstanding.

rows.text: Ryan sent me word at midnight that he must speak with me, and I knew at once what such a message meant, as such messages generally do.

notes.after: and I knew at once what such a message meant, as such messages generally do

notes.text: a framing generalization the matter invites, laying the narrator's dry judgement over her own case, in her usual way of irony
notes.after: as such messages generally do

rows.text: We met the next day at a coffee house in the town, where he was already seated, and so busy over the instrument in his hand that he did not at first perceive me. He looked nervous, and in the same breath professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his own.
I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded and said that it was all right, and then walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

notes.after: I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded and said that it was all right

rows.text: My friend was of opinion that I made too much of the business; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me notwithstanding.

lessons: Their passage tells the matter in bare, unjoined sentences, where Austen gathers the event, its meaning, and the narrator's judgement into one balanced period. I joined the three opening sentences into a single period ending on the general truth "as such messages generally do," which lets the narrator's dry irony land without adding any new feeling. His speech is reported rather than quoted ("he professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment"), and her composure is shown by conduct ("I only nodded") rather than named; practise joining your clauses with "and" and "but" so that the main point arrives late, and let feeling show in what people do.

the meeting at the coffee shop and what he said
walking home in the rain, ice cream, the narrator's composure
her roommate's verdict, her own doubt, and the hurt

plan.why: open with the event and let the narrator's knowledge of its meaning land in a period that ends hard

plan.why: give feeling by conduct and countenance, and report his speech in the narrator's syntax

faults.quote: "so busy over the instrument in his hand that he did not at first perceive me"
faults.why: The draft says only that Ryan was scrolling on his phone. It does not say that he failed to notice the narrator, even briefly; this invents a small action and changes the social texture of the meeting.

faults.quote: "in the same breath professed"
faults.why: “In the same breath” adds a timing and manner not present in the two reported statements, while “professed” makes Ryan sound affected, doubtful, or insincere. The original neutrally says that he said these things.

faults.quote: "My friend was of opinion"
faults.why: The roommate is changed into a friend. A roommate is a specific relation and part of the original situation; the rewrite drops that fact.

faults.quote: "at a coffee house in the town"
faults.why: This generalizes away the specified downtown location. “In the town” is not necessarily equivalent to downtown and loses a concrete setting detail.

faults.quote: "the instrument in his hand"
faults.why: This is not a natural Austen-like way to accommodate a phone. “Instrument” ordinarily suggests a musical instrument, scientific implement, or tool, so it reads as conspicuous pseudo-period evasion rather than Austen’s precise social narration.

faults.quote: "the instrument in his hand"
faults.why: The phrase is needlessly riddle-like: a reader has to infer that the instrument is a phone, and its association with scrolling is awkward.

faults.quote: "cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 33, ¶ 38" and "cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 18, ¶ 9"
faults.why: The paragraph citations are not verifiable without an edition, since paragraph numbering varies, and the notes do not quote or explain the relevant Austen passage. They therefore do not give the writer an apt, usable source for the claimed moves.

faults.quote: "His speech is reported rather than quoted"
faults.why: This describes no real revision: the writer’s original already reports Ryan’s speech indirectly (“He said...”), rather than quoting it. The lesson inaccurately credits the rewrite with a change it did not make.

faults.quote: "her composure is shown by conduct ... rather than named"
faults.why: The original already shows the narrator’s composure through conduct: “I just nodded and said okay.” The lesson misses the actual stylistic alteration—chiefly compression and diction—and consequently gives misleading revision advice.

faults.quote: "without adding any new feeling"
faults.why: The added phrase “as such messages generally do” supplies a dry generalized irony absent from the plainer original. Such commentary may be a permissible voice liberty, but the lesson should acknowledge it rather than claim that no feeling was added.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the central sequence and is generally intelligible, but it loses the roommate detail and introduces several unnecessary interpretive embellishments. Its Austen effect is strongest in its balanced sentences, yet weakened by evasive pseudo-period diction and notes that misdescribe several of the actual changes.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children. The father seemed an amiable man; his sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast.

My mother, who could never rest till she knew the whole of any new arrival, carried over a plate of biscuits almost before the family had done taking out. She meant to learn where they came from, what the father did for a living, and whether they went to church, and she did not return till she had satisfied herself on every one of these points.

It was soon learnt that the father was a lawyer, and that he was a single man; that is to say, he had been parted from his wife. My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to settle me for years.

rows.text: A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children. The father seemed an amiable man; his sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast.

notes.text: The first paragraph gives the household a mother and father together — 'The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish' — so the 'mom' first reads as the father's wife; the last paragraph then says the dad is 'single. Well, divorced.' I made the standoffish woman the father's sister who shares his house: the household keeps a second adult, the narrator's mother still has someone to receive her, and nothing said of her (her coolness, her place in the house) conflicts with her being a sister, whereas a wife cannot stand beside 'single.'
notes.after: The father seemed an amiable man. His sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast.

rows.text: My mother, who could never rest till she knew the whole of any new arrival, carried over a plate of biscuits almost before the family had done taking out. She meant to learn where they came from, what the father did for a living, and whether they went to church, and she did not return till she had satisfied herself on every one of these points.

It was soon learnt that the father was a lawyer, and that he was a single man; that is to say, he had been parted from his wife. My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to settle me for years.

notes.text: The passage echoes Pride and Prejudice's opening: a new household arrives, and a mother schemes to marry her child to the eligible man in it. The rewrite takes the method of showing the mother's scheme through busy neighbourly conduct (the biscuits standing in for the visit of introduction) and through the child's dry, knowing narration; it also keeps the man's eligibility — lawyer, divorced — established before the mother's look, so the look has its cause, as Mrs Bennet acts only on a confirmed single man of fortune.
notes.after: My mother would not lose a moment in carrying over a plate of biscuits … It was soon learnt that the father was a lawyer, and parted from his wife. My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake.
My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking.

notes.text: The voice lets the narrator, looking back, judge the mother's scheme dryly in a brief closing clause, as Austen's children-narrators report a parent's designs; it adds no new incident, only the knowing frame the passage itself invites by ending on the set-up.
notes.after: which I had too often seen to mistake

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage names each plain fact in a short, unjudging sentence, while Austen builds long periods that let the narrator judge as she tells. Most of my sentences join two of yours with a semicolon, and the judgement comes in her abstract nouns — 'an amiable man', 'a colder cast' — so the reader feels the narrator's dry eye on the mother long before the close. Practise the balanced period ('A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children') and the verdict by understatement ('She has been trying to settle me for years', whose 'settle' keeps the comic distance without a single modern phrase).

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the household a mother and father together — “The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish” — so the “mom” first read as the father's wife; your last paragraph then says the dad is “single. Well, divorced.”
sense.quote: The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the standoffish woman the father's sister, not his wife: “The dad seems nice. His sister, who lives with him, is kind of standoffish.” — the least change, since the household keeps a second adult, the narrator's mother still has someone to be received by, and nothing said of her (coolness, sharing the house) conflicts with her being a sister, whereas wife cannot stand beside “single.”

sense.problem: A true echo: a new household arrives in the neighbourhood and a mother schemes to marry her child to the eligible man in it.
sense.quote: A new family moved in next door last weekend. … My mom got this look on her face. … She has been trying to set me up for years.
sense.resolution: Pride and Prejudice, opening: the arrival of a single man of good fortune and a mother's campaign to secure him. The rewrite may take from it the method of letting the mother's scheme show through busy neighbourly action (the cookies standing in for the visit of introduction), and the habit of reporting the parent's designs through the child's dry, knowing narration — but it must earn the eligibility: Austen's Mrs Bennet acts on a confirmed single man of fortune, so keep “lawyer” and “divorced” before the look, never after it.

faults.quote: with a large cart
faults.why: This does not retain the detail that the family have a “huge truck.” A cart is not necessarily large, and the modern truck has been reduced to a vaguer period substitute.

faults.quote: carried over a plate of biscuits
faults.why: The original specifically says that the narrator’s mother baked cookies. Carrying biscuits over omits the baking and substitutes a different action.

faults.quote: she did not return till she had satisfied herself on every one of these points
faults.why: This adds a definite incident and outcome: an extended visit, her return, and her successful discovery of every answer. The draft says only that she wanted to find out everything.

faults.quote: his sister, who keeps his house
faults.why: Identifying the woman as a sister is a defensible repair of the stated contradiction, but “who keeps his house” adds a domestic role not supplied by the draft and not necessary to make the repair.

faults.quote: almost before the family had done taking out
faults.why: “Had done taking out” is incomplete and awkward: taking out what is never supplied. It does not read as idiomatic Austenian prose; “unpacking” or a specified object would be needed.

faults.quote: My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look
faults.why: A countenance may assume, wear, or betray an expression, but “took a look” is stiff and unnatural. It sounds like a mechanical imitation of nineteenth-century diction.

faults.quote: that is to say, he had been parted from his wife
faults.why: This is less precise and less idiomatic than Austen’s usual social vocabulary for divorce or separation. It also weakens the crisp comic correction in “single. Well, divorced” without finding an equally pointed Austenian equivalent.

faults.quote: “My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking.” — cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 22, ¶ 40
faults.why: The cited sentence is presented as a source-based move, but the wording does not identify an apt, recognizable Austen parallel and appears to be the rewrite’s own awkward phrasing rather than a reliable quotation or close textual model. The note should cite an actual comparable construction and explain the relevant technique.

faults.quote: as Mrs Bennet acts only on a confirmed single man of fortune
faults.why: This is not an accurate description of Mrs Bennet’s conduct in Pride and Prejudice. Her interest begins on hearing that Bingley is a wealthy single man; the claim that she acts only after confirmation is both overstated and unnecessary.

faults.quote: it adds no new incident
faults.why: This is inaccurate. The rewrite adds that the mother made the visit before unpacking was complete, remained until she had obtained all the information, and then returned. Those are new narrated events, not merely a knowing frame.

faults.quote: Most of my sentences join two of yours with a semicolon
faults.why: The lesson misdescribes the rewrite. Only the first paragraph’s second sentence prominently uses a semicolon; the rewrite does not mostly join the draft’s sentences this way.

faults.quote: Practise the balanced period ('A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children')
faults.why: The quoted sentence is not a notably balanced period; it is a straightforward main clause followed by an appended phrase. Calling it a balanced period gives the writer an imprecise model for a reusable syntactic technique.

judge.verdict: The rewrite correctly identifies and repairs the draft’s central contradiction, and its broad sequence remains intact. But it loses concrete details, adds unreported events, and is weakened by several un-Austenian or unidiomatic phrases and inaccurate explanatory notes.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
To all who are concerned in the undertaking,

The setting up, which was to have been on Tuesday, is now fixed for Thursday; for the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices, and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature.

I must beg that each of you will have your several parts of the papers ready by noon on Wednesday; and whoever among you is at a stand, let him tell me of it today, and not tomorrow.

With thanks, Sam.

rows.text: To all who are concerned in the undertaking,

notes.text: The writer's bare 'Hi team' becomes a formal address; the voice names the persons by what they are about rather than by a modern word, which is her way of opening a note of business.
notes.after: To all who are concerned in the undertaking,

rows.text: The setting up, which was to have been on Tuesday, is now fixed for Thursday; for the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices, and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature.

notes.after: for the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices, and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature.

notes.text: The voice frames the bare change of day as a matter appointed and then altered, giving the news its due weight in one balanced period rather than two staccato clauses.
notes.after: which was to have been on Tuesday, is now fixed for Thursday

rows.text: I must beg that each of you will have your several parts of the papers ready by noon on Wednesday; and whoever among you is at a stand, let him tell me of it today, and not tomorrow.
With thanks, Sam.

lessons: Your note commands and staccatos; the author's manner joins each fact to its cause and its condition in one balanced period, so that the delay and its reason arrive together ("for the lawyers have not yet signed... and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature"). She turns bare commands into reported entreaties ("I must beg that each of you...") and lets the warning land by understatement ("at a stand... and not tomorrow"), which the reader feels as courtesy rather than office pressure. Practise joining two of your short sentences with "for" or "; and", and putting a request as what you "beg" rather than what you order.

reading.kind: letter (a brief business note of news, reason, request, and close)

outline.gist: Address the team
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed the pricing page; do not ship without it
Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
If blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow
Thanks, Sam

plan.gist: Address the persons concerned in the undertaking
plan.why: A note of business opens on its company, as a letter opens on its reader; the voice names the persons rather than the modern 'team'.

plan.gist: The delay, and the cause of it, in one period
plan.why: Her periods join the fact and its cause with 'for', the news first and the reason following, so the reader takes the whole matter at once.

plan.gist: The readiness of the papers, and the warning against silence
plan.why: The request is put as a reported entreaty rather than a bare command, and the condition attached to it, so the two turn on one point of time.

plan.gist: Thanks, with the name
plan.why: Her letters end on a short courteous line, the thanks and the name standing alone.

faults.quote: “The setting up”
faults.why: This is not a reliable equivalent for a product or project launch. “Setting up” suggests arranging or establishing something, rather than releasing it; the specific event being delayed is blurred.

faults.quote: “the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices”
faults.why: This narrows and alters “Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page.” A legal department need not be individual lawyers, “signed off” is approval rather than necessarily a signature, and a pricing page is not merely a list of prices.

faults.quote: “I would not send it abroad”
faults.why: This recasts the modern product-release sense of “shipping” as sending a physical item out into the world. It is a plausible periodizing gesture, but it loses the release/publication nuance of the original.

faults.quote: “your several parts of the papers”
faults.why: The deck is changed into “papers.” That is understandable as an adaptation, but a presentation deck and a set of papers are not necessarily the same thing, so the requested deliverable is less precise.

faults.quote: “To all who are concerned in the undertaking”
faults.why: The address sounds like a proclamation, circular, or legal notice more than Austen’s characteristic letter openings. It is formal without acquiring the particular intimacy, irony, or social precision of her epistolary voice.

faults.quote: “The setting up, which was to have been on Tuesday”
faults.why: The phrasing is merely archaising and is not convincingly Austenian. “Setting up” is especially weak diction here; it produces a costume-period effect rather than an idiomatic Austen equivalent for a launch.

faults.quote: “while it wanted that signature”
faults.why: Although “want” can historically mean “lack,” the phrase makes the pricing material seem to require a literal signature. The intended meaning is approval from Legal, and the sentence therefore sounds stilted as well as less exact.

faults.quote: “whoever among you is at a stand, let him tell me of it today”
faults.why: “At a stand” is comprehensible, but the combination with “let him tell me of it” is awkwardly bureaucratic. It does not have the ease of Austen’s letters and unnecessarily imposes a masculine singular on an unspecified team.

faults.quote: “— cites Persuasion, ch. 9, ¶ 29”
faults.why: This is not a useful or verifiable source note. Paragraph numbering differs by edition, and the note gives neither an Austen quotation nor an explanation of what exact syntactic or rhetorical feature is being borrowed from that passage.

faults.quote: “Paragraph 3: (no notes)”
faults.why: The rewrite makes a substantive adaptation here—“sections of the deck” becomes “several parts of the papers”—but does not acknowledge or justify it. Since the tool is required to preserve a work email’s requests precisely, this liberty should be identified.

faults.quote: “Paragraph 4: (no notes)”
faults.why: This paragraph changes “If you're blocked” into “whoever among you is at a stand” and changes the grammatical gender. These are consequential diction and register choices, yet the notes provide no account of them.

faults.quote: “Your note commands and staccatos”
faults.why: This is both imprecise and needlessly dismissive of the original’s efficient work-email style. The writer’s short sentences are clear and appropriately urgent; the lesson should distinguish a deliberate modern business rhythm from a stylistic defect.

faults.quote: “Practise joining two of your short sentences with ‘for’ or ‘; and’”
faults.why: The advice risks teaching a mechanical period mannerism rather than a transferable principle. It should explain when joining clauses improves causality or tonal control, and when concise separate sentences are better—especially in an email with deadlines.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the overall sequence and the two requests, but several substitutions make the business facts less exact and the Austen effect is mostly generic archaism. Its structure is sound, while the notes and lesson need more accurate sourcing and more useful guidance about when, rather than merely how, to adopt the borrowed moves.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to carriages on the days of rest. To put a carriage anywhere in the town is a thing of no small difficulty, and the pavements are too narrow for the carriages of children; other places have made the trial, and their shopkeepers are doing better than they have ever done before.

Some persons in trade will complain that their customers cannot reach them; but they will grow accustomed to it. Most people walk from the carriage-house already, in truth.

We should make the trial this summer.

faults.quote: "carriages"
faults.why: Replacing cars with horse-drawn carriages changes the subject of the proposal and the practical conditions on which the argument rests. An Austen-like syntax could retain the fact of cars rather than historicizing it.

faults.quote: "on the days of rest"
faults.why: “Weekends” ordinarily means Saturday and Sunday, whereas “days of rest” has a Sabbath-like sense and can suggest only Sunday. This alters the proposed schedule.

faults.quote: "To put a carriage anywhere in the town"
faults.why: The original concern is parking downtown. “Anywhere in the town” broadens both the geographical scope and the inconvenience being asserted.

faults.quote: "the pavements are too narrow for the carriages of children"
faults.why: This does not clearly mean strollers. It can mean carriages owned or operated by children, producing an unintendedly comic and unclear image; it also substitutes a different conveyance for the stated one.

faults.quote: "a thing of no small difficulty"
faults.why: The original calls parking “a nightmare,” a strongly negative evaluation. This genteel litotes substantially softens its force rather than preserving the degree of frustration.

faults.quote: "the carriages of children"
faults.why: The phrase is not idiomatic for child strollers and is especially awkward in the proposed historical register. “Children’s carriages” would at least identify the intended object, though it would still alter the modern fact.

faults.quote: "close Main Street to carriages on the days of rest"
faults.why: The passage relies chiefly on replacing modern nouns with pseudo-period equivalents. That is costume rather than a convincing Austenian transformation of syntax, social observation, and controlled irony.

faults.quote: "the voice strengthens it so the improvement sounds the greater"
faults.why: The rewrite says shopkeepers are “doing better than they have ever done before,” which means the same thing as “doing better than ever.” The note describes an intensification that did not occur and improperly characterizes it as a permissible liberty.

faults.quote: "The writer's: claim (Main Street should be closed to carriages on the days of rest)"
faults.why: The structural explanation silently rewrites the writer’s actual “cars on weekends” as the altered “carriages on the days of rest.” It should identify and justify any change, not present it as the source text.

faults.quote: "the town should deny its principal street to carriages"
faults.why: The outline replaces the specific name “Main Street” with the generic “its principal street.” This is another unreported factual substitution and is not the wording used in the rewrite itself.

faults.quote: "I joined your three short middle sentences"
faults.why: The three sentences joined are the opening paragraph’s sentences, not “middle sentences.” More importantly, the lesson treats historical substitutions as a stylistic technique without warning that they changed the writer’s facts.

faults.quote: "Practise building one period that holds complaint and answer together"
faults.why: This advice is only loosely grounded in the revision: the original already puts the business objection and its answer together in one sentence. The lesson does not clearly distinguish what structural improvement was made from what was already present.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the broad argumentative sequence, but it repeatedly changes modern facts to create a period costume and introduces an unclear phrase about children’s carriages. Its notes and lesson compound the problem by treating those alterations as if they were in the original and by inaccurately claiming an intensification.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we should alter the week to four days. The people are worn out, and our best engineer has just left us; and it cannot but be felt that there are studies which show the work going on as well, or better, under such an arrangement. It would help us, too, in the engaging of new people; it would render us the more desirable.

I know it is a wild scheme, and that our clients might not like it; but we might try it for three months, and then judge.

notes.after: it would render us the more desirable

rows.text: I know it is a wild scheme, and that our clients might not like it; but we might try it for three months, and then judge.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's page is a list of plain clauses, where the author builds one or two full periods whose clauses balance and whose verdicts arrive late. I joined the two reasons into one sentence on a semicolon, turned the bare benefit into its consequence with abstract nouns ('it would render us the more desirable'), and closed the objection with her understatement ('a wild scheme... try it for three months, and then judge'); practise balancing an objection and its answer in a single period, and letting the narrator's nouns of judgement carry the weight of feeling.

faults.quote: "I know it is a wild scheme"
faults.why: “Wild” is substantially stronger and more dismissive than the writer’s “risky.” It changes the degree of the speaker’s concession rather than merely giving it an Austen-like phrasing.

faults.quote: "there are studies which show the work going on as well, or better"
faults.why: This blurs the specific claim that productivity stays the same or increases. “The work going on” can mean merely that work continues, not that output/productivity is maintained or improved.

faults.quote: "it cannot but be felt that there are studies"
faults.why: The construction makes the point an impersonal feeling that studies exist, rather than the writer’s direct evidentiary assertion that studies show a particular result. It is also unclear who is doing the feeling and why that is relevant.

faults.quote: "alter the week to four days"
faults.why: This is not an idiomatic way to express adopting a four-day workweek. It sounds mechanically archaic rather than like a natural Austen sentence.

faults.quote: "the engaging of new people; it would render us the more desirable"
faults.why: “Engaging” is a possible historical word for employing, but “new people” and “render us the more desirable” are vague and awkward together. The comparative “the more desirable” lacks a clear comparison and produces a strained corporate paraphrase.

faults.quote: "The people are worn out"
faults.why: The sentence has a generalized, contemporary workplace register without Austen’s usual social precision, ironic qualification, or character-inflected judgement. The surrounding archaisms do not fully make it sound like her prose.

faults.quote: "cites Emma, ch. 29, ¶ 10"
faults.why: The note gives a highly specific citation without identifying the borrowed wording or explaining how the cited passage supports this particular syntactic move. Paragraph numbering is edition-dependent, and the citation is not useful to the writer as presented.

faults.quote: "Paragraph 2: (no notes)"
faults.why: The second paragraph makes a consequential change—“risky” becomes “a wild scheme”—but supplies no note acknowledging or defending that alteration. Since it changes the force of the objection, it should have been reported.

faults.quote: "I joined the two reasons into one sentence on a semicolon"
faults.why: This inaccurately describes the revision: the long sentence combines burnout, the engineer’s departure, and the studies; the hiring reason remains in a separate sentence. The lesson therefore gives the writer an imprecise account of the structural move.

faults.quote: "her understatement ('a wild scheme... try it for three months, and then judge')"
faults.why: Calling “a wild scheme” understatement is misleading. It intensifies the writer’s “risky” into a more dramatic judgement, so it is not a reliable lesson in how to calibrate an objection.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the argument’s overall sequence and all of its major elements, but it weakens the productivity evidence and overstates the risk. It has some Austen-like balancing and diction, yet several phrases feel like modern business prose dressed in archaism, while the notes overclaim and fail to account for the strongest semantic change.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all put out by it. In truth, my relief was as great as it was unworthy; for I had been dreading the engagement the whole week past, and I am far from proud of that.

I told her it was perfectly fine, and that we should do it another time. But I do not think we shall.

rows.text: When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all put out by it. In truth, my relief was as great as it was unworthy; for I had been dreading the engagement the whole week past, and I am far from proud of that.

notes.after: for I had been dreading the engagement the whole week past, and I am far from proud of that.

notes.text: the narrator looks back and judges her own feeling, as Austen's first-person narrators do; the writer said only that she was relieved and not proud, and the voice frames both in one abstract phrase
notes.after: my relief was as great as it was unworthy

rows.text: I told her it was perfectly fine, and that we should do it another time. But I do not think we shall.

lessons: Your passage names a feeling plainly in short sentences; Austen's manner is to hold several clauses in one period and let the feeling be judged rather than merely stated. "My relief was as great as it was unworthy" joins the relief and the shame in a single balanced phrase, and the closing "But I do not think we shall" works because the short sentence is saved for the deflating turn. Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" or a semicolon, and letting the main point arrive late in the sentence.

faults.quote: When Dana put off our dinner
faults.why: “Put off” means postponed, whereas “cancelled” can mean calling off the arrangement altogether. The following promise to do it another time makes postponement plausible, but the replacement still narrows and slightly changes the event.

faults.quote: my relief was as great as it was unworthy
faults.why: The original says the narrator was relieved and ashamed of that relief; it does not say that the shame or unworthiness was equal in degree to the relief. The balanced comparison adds a precise emotional proportion.

faults.quote: I told her it was perfectly fine, and that we should do it another time.
faults.why: “Perfectly fine” and “do it another time” retain a fairly modern conversational register. The sentence has some period surface, but its diction does not consistently sound like Austen’s prose.

faults.quote: as Austen's first-person narrators do
faults.why: This is an inaccurate generalization. Austen’s major novels are principally third-person narrated, often in free indirect style; first-person writing is more characteristic of her letters and some juvenilia. The note should identify a relevant mode or source rather than claim a general first-person-narrator practice.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the narrator looks back and judges her own feeling
faults.why: This is not a liberty beyond the source. The writer already judges the feeling directly in “I'm not proud of that.” The note incorrectly describes an existing element as an addition, and it overlooks that the rewrite also changes the degree through “as great as it was unworthy.”

faults.quote: cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 12, ¶ 29
faults.why: The note gives a location but does not quote or explain the Austen construction being borrowed. Since the cited wording is not shown, the writer cannot test the claimed model or learn what feature of it—syntax, antithesis, narrative judgment—is being adapted.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" or a semicolon
faults.why: This reduces the lesson to punctuation and risks teaching an Austen costume rather than a transferable rhetorical choice. It should explain when clauses belong in one sentence—for example, when a later clause revises or morally qualifies the earlier feeling—and distinguish that from merely lengthening sentences.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the central emotional direction and its compact two-paragraph movement well, but it makes a small change to the cancellation and adds an equal-degree judgment. Its Austen effect is partial, while the notes contain a significant factual overstatement about Austen’s narration and do not adequately substantiate their source claim.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant.

And it came to pass on the morrow, that we met at a coffee store in the midst of the city; and he was there before me, moving over the charger of his phone. And his countenance was troubled, and he was sore ill at ease. And he said unto me, I am not ready for that which is weighty: and he said, It is not thou, it is I.

And I would have wept, but I wept not: for I bowed my head and said, It is well. And I went home in the rain, and I ate a whole measure of ice cream.

And my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter. Peradventure I did: but it grieved me still.

rows.text: And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant.

notes.text: No fault of sense: Ryan, the narrator, and the roommate are consistent, and the order of events is clear. Nothing to mend. Nothing changed for sense.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant.

And his countenance was troubled, and he was sore ill at ease. And he said unto me, I am not ready for that which is weighty: and he said, It is not thou, it is I.

notes.text: The passage echoes, faintly, the scene of Ruth's refusal to leave ('whither thou goest, I will go', Ruth 1), but inverted: here it is the other who leaves, and the narrator is the one told to go. The prodigal son (Luke 15) is weaker: the narrator comes home to ice cream and a roommate's judgment, not to a welcome. The rewrite may take from Ruth the plain, bare dialogue and the grief carried in the going, but must not import Ruth's fidelity; the story's point is its opposite.

notes.text: The voice frames the old cliché in its own words, giving the verdict plainly without the writer's modern idiom; the framing is the voice's, the fact is the writer's.
notes.after: and he said, It is not thou, it is I

rows.text: And I would have wept, but I wept not: for I bowed my head and said, It is well. And I went home in the rain, and I ate a whole measure of ice cream.
And my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter. Peradventure I did: but it grieved me still.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short, clipped sentences become long sentences built of clauses joined by 'and', so that the grief is carried in the going rather than stated. My rewrite joins the message and the foreboding into one movement ('And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant'), and gives feeling by its sign rather than its name ('I would have wept, but I wept not', 'my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter'). Practise laying clause beside clause with 'and', and giving the sign of a feeling in short, old, concrete words, so that the reader carries the weight instead of being told to.

plan.why: the voice lays one clause beside another with 'and', so the message and the foreboding land together as one continuous movement

plan.gist: the setting the next day, then the man found already there
plan.why: the setting comes before the scene, and the man is found where the voice first sees him, with no waste

plan.gist: his words given in full, plainly, with the two halves parallel
plan.why: the voice brings speech in by 'said unto' and gives it whole; the doubled refusal echoes the writer's two sentences

plan.why: feeling is given by its sign, gravely; the walk and the ice cream are one sentence joined by 'and', so the grief is carried in the going, as in Ruth

plan.gist: the roommate's judgment, the narrator's half-yielding, and the closing hurt
plan.why: the verdict of another, then the brief self-doubt, then the short sentence that closes: the point lands hardest at the end

sense.problem: No fault of sense: no contradiction, no unclear person or time, no missing step the reader needs. Ryan, the narrator, and the roommate are consistent throughout, and the sequence noon-to-afternoon is clear.

Echo: the passage echoes, faintly, the scene of the servant who refuses to leave — 'whither thou goest, I will go' (Ruth 1) — but inverted: here it is the other who leaves, and the narrator is the one told to go. The prodigal son (Luke 15) is a weaker echo: the narrator comes home to ice cream and a roommate's judgment, not to a welcome.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from Ruth the plain, bare dialogue and the steadfast refusal to dramatize — words spoken and kept, grief carried in the going — but must not import Ruth's fidelity; the story's point is its opposite.
sense.quote: He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

faults.quote: Ryan sent word unto me
faults.why: This removes the specific fact that Ryan texted. A biblicalized rendering can retain the medium more closely (for example, by making clear that the message came through his phone), whereas “sent word” is a more general and different act.

faults.quote: moving over the charger of his phone
faults.why: This does not preserve “scrolling on his phone.” A charger is not the phone's screen or its contents, so the concrete action is lost.

faults.quote: moving over the charger of his phone
faults.why: The phrase is unclear: it could mean handling a charging cable, moving physically over it, or scrolling through something called a charger. It does not yield the intended action without guesswork.

faults.quote: moving over the charger of his phone
faults.why: “Moving over” is not idiomatic for scrolling, and “charger” is used in a plainly wrong or at least highly confusing sense.

faults.quote: I am not ready for that which is weighty
faults.why: “That which is weighty” is a stiff abstraction rather than natural biblical diction for a serious relationship or commitment. It sounds like a thesaurus substitution, not a phrase with the plain force of the King James Bible.

faults.quote: I bowed my head and said, It is well
faults.why: Bowing one's head is not necessarily nodding, and “It is well” means substantially more than “okay”: it declares that matters are well rather than merely acknowledging what Ryan has said. This strengthens and changes the narrator's response.

faults.quote: I ate a whole measure of ice cream
faults.why: The specific fact that the narrator ate a whole pint is reduced to an unspecified “measure.” The rewrite need not use modern packaging language exactly, but it should preserve the quantity more distinctly.

faults.quote: a whole measure of ice cream
faults.why: “Measure” is vague and unnatural as a container or serving of ice cream. It reads as an evasive archaism rather than a usable sentence.

faults.quote: my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart
faults.why: The original gives no gender for the roommate, but the rewrite invents “her.” It also turns the roommate's thought into an interior statement; that is a possible rendering of “thought,” but the added gender is not.

faults.quote: No fault of sense: Ryan, the narrator, and the roommate are consistent, and the order of events is clear. Nothing to mend. Nothing changed for sense.
faults.why: This is inaccurate as a report on the rewrite. The rewrite assigns the roommate a gender and introduces the unclear “charger” phrase; at minimum those changes should have been acknowledged rather than declaring that nothing changed.

faults.quote: here it is the other who leaves, and the narrator is the one told to go
faults.why: Neither the source nor the rewrite says Ryan tells the narrator to leave. This imports a nonexistent incident and misdescribes the passage while claiming to explain its handling.

faults.quote: The prodigal son (Luke 15) is weaker: the narrator comes home to ice cream and a roommate's judgment, not to a welcome.
faults.why: This is an elaborate but unhelpful allusion that does not identify a rewriting move. It distracts from the actual textual issues and risks teaching the writer to manufacture biblical parallels instead of learning syntax, diction, and narrative compression.

faults.quote: cites 1 Kings 17:2
faults.why: 1 Kings 17:2 is chiefly a formula for the word of the Lord coming to Elijah; it is not an apt or specific source for the claimed technique of laying successive narrative clauses beside one another with “and.”

faults.quote: cites 2 Samuel 15:26
faults.why: 2 Samuel 15:26 does not provide the stated parallel construction, “It is not thou, it is I.” The citation is not a reliable source for the move it is said to illustrate.

faults.quote: Paragraph 3: (no notes)
faults.why: The response paragraph contains consequential substitutions—especially “I would have wept,” “bowed my head,” “It is well,” and “a whole measure”—but the notes give the writer no account of those choices or of their losses in precision.

faults.quote: Paragraph 4: (no notes)
faults.why: The final paragraph silently introduces the roommate's gender and changes “thought I was overreacting” into “said in her heart.” The omission is especially problematic because the earlier sense note falsely says nothing changed.

faults.quote: giving the sign of a feeling in short, old, concrete words
faults.why: This is a potentially useful principle, but it is undercut by examples such as “that which is weighty” and “a whole measure,” which are abstract or vague rather than concrete. The lesson does not teach how to preserve a modern detail precisely while changing register.

judge.verdict: The overall sequence and much of the biblical cadence are retained, but several details are blurred or altered, and “charger of his phone” is both a sense failure and an unidiomatic phrase. The notes are the chief weakness: they deny real changes, make a false Ruth-based claim, and supply poorly matched citations.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours, with a great truck and two little children. And the father of them seemed good: and his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near.

And my mother baked them cakes straightway, for she desired to know all their matters: whence they came, and what they did for their work, and whether they went up to the house of God.

And it came to pass that the father of them was a lawyer and had put away his wife, and was single. And a look came upon the face of my mother, and I knew the thought of her heart: for she hath sought these many years to set me unto a man.

rows.text: And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours, with a great truck and two little children. And the father of them seemed good: and his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother — 'The mom is kind of standoffish' — but your third says of the same household that 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A single, divorced father cannot at once have a wife; and nothing tells the reader who the standoffish one is. I made the standoffish one his sister who came with him, the least change that lets the father stay single and divorced, which the mother's scheming over him requires.
notes.after: And his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near.

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences run very short and modern, where the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with 'and' until each sentence carries a whole turn of the matter. I opened your story with 'And it came to pass', joined your three neighbourly questions with 'and' into one breath, and made the standoffish one the father's sister so the divorce stands. Practise giving feeling by its sign — 'a look came upon the face of my mother' — rather than by telling, and joining deeds with their reasons in one long sentence, for that is how this voice lets a scene gather weight.

plan.gist: The new family comes next door with a great truck and two little children
plan.why: The voice opens a scene with 'it came to pass' and lays thing beside thing with 'and' before any judgment

plan.gist: The father seemeth good, and the one with him is aloof
plan.why: The voice gives the report of character plainly, and the mending makes the aloof one the sister so the father may stand single later

plan.gist: The mother baketh cakes straightway, desiring to know all of them
plan.why: The voice tells the neighbourly kindness and the prying in one breath, the motive after the deed

plan.gist: The father is a lawyer and put away from his wife
plan.why: The voice turns the finding with 'and it came to pass', and tells the divorce as plain fact

plan.gist: The mother's countenance; the narrator knoweth her mind and her long scheming
plan.why: The voice closes with the weightiest point last, the sign of a face and years of purpose

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother: 'The mom is kind of standoffish.' Your third paragraph says of the same household that 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A man who is single — divorced — cannot at the same time have a wife who is the mom of his household; and nothing tells the reader who this mom is.
sense.resolution: Make the standoffish one not the father's wife: since the household is a single divorced father's with two little kids, she is most fitly his sister who lives with him, or the children's grandmother — the least change is 'His sister is kind of standoffish.' Then the dad may be divorced and single, and the mother's scheming over him stands. (If you would rather keep a mom, the mending must go the other way — the dad is married — but that undoes the whole point about setting you up, so the passage itself points to the sister.)
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours
faults.why: This omits “last weekend,” a concrete time marker in the original. The setting is therefore not fully retained.

faults.quote: And my mother baked them cakes straightway
faults.why: “Cakes” is not the same thing as cookies. Biblicalizing the diction does not require changing the food, and the notes do not acknowledge this alteration.

faults.quote: his sister that was with him was aloof
faults.why: The required sense-mending permits making the apparent mother another woman in the household, but specifying that she is his sister invents a relationship unsupported by the draft. A less committal repair could have avoided this added fact.

faults.quote: the father of them seemed good
faults.why: “Nice” is a limited social impression; “good” can carry a broader moral judgment in biblical diction. The rewrite slightly strengthens the narrator’s evaluation.

faults.quote: whether they went up to the house of God
faults.why: This changes the question of whether they “went to church” into whether they went up to a particular house of God. The former concerns religious attendance or affiliation; the latter suggests a journey to a sacred building.

faults.quote: his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near
faults.why: “Aloof” is conspicuously modern and does not sound like King James Bible diction. “Unto them that drew near” is appended in a way that feels like biblical costume rather than a natural scriptural sentence.

faults.quote: the father of them
faults.why: This is understandable but ungainly. The King James Bible more naturally uses possessives such as “their father” where the relation is this simple.

faults.quote: And a look came upon the face of my mother
faults.why: The phrase is syntactically intelligible but not idiomatic KJV phrasing. Biblical narration would more naturally speak of a face or countenance changing, falling, or being lifted up, rather than a look “coming upon” it.

faults.quote: she hath sought these many years to set me unto a man
faults.why: “Set me unto a man” is not a natural King James idiom for matchmaking. It also makes the intended romantic arrangement slightly less clear than the original’s “set me up.”

faults.quote: And it came to pass: “And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell...” — cites Ruth 1:19
faults.why: Ruth 1:19 does not contain “And it came to pass”; it begins, “So they two went until they came to Bethlehem.” The citation does not support the identified move.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near” — cites 1 Samuel 17:41
faults.why: 1 Samuel 17:41 describes the Philistine drawing near to David and the shield-bearer going before him. It is not an apt source for this sentence’s alleged parallelism or for its diction.

faults.quote: Clauses laid side by side with “and” ... — cites Mark 5:14
faults.why: Mark 5:14 does use repeated conjunctions, but it does not closely support the three-part interrogative catalogue being described. The source is too loose to be useful teaching evidence.

faults.quote: A single, divorced father cannot at once have a wife; and nothing tells the reader who the standoffish one is.
faults.why: The note identifies the real contradiction but describes it inaccurately. The draft explicitly identifies the standoffish person as “The mom”; the problem is that this apparent current mother conflicts with the later description of the father as single and divorced, not that her identity is unstated.

faults.quote: the least change that lets the father stay single and divorced
faults.why: Making the woman specifically “his sister” is not the least change. It adds an unprovided familial relation rather than simply revising the ambiguous “mom” into an unspecified woman in the household.

faults.quote: Practise giving feeling by its sign — 'a look came upon the face of my mother'

faults.quote: The writer's: ... scout (The dad seems nice; the standoffish one is not his wife)
faults.why: This falsely attributes the repair to the writer’s original structure. The original calls the standoffish person “The mom”; it does not say, imply clearly, or establish that she is not the father’s wife.

faults.quote: setting (A new family moved in next door last weekend...)

faults.quote: The father seemeth good

lessons: Your note is hurried and telegraphic; the author's manner is slow and full, clause laid beside clause. I opened the letter with a salutation ("Unto the team, greeting") and joined your news to its cause with "for," so the reading moves as the Bible moves. Your charge I doubled into parallel halves ("let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow"), which gives the command weight and a place to land. Practise laying one clause against another with "and" and "for" instead of stacking short sentences.

the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday

plan.why: the epistle opens with a direct salutation, as Paul's letters do

plan.gist: the launch moves to Thursday
plan.why: the news comes first, plainly, before the reason for it

plan.gist: the lawyers have not approved the pricing page, and he will not go without it

plan.why: the epistle ends with thanks and the sender's own hand

faults.quote: "the launch passeth from the second day unto the fourth day of the week"
faults.why: This does not securely preserve Tuesday-to-Thursday. If Tuesday is called the second day, Wednesday is necessarily the third; the later dating of the Wednesday deadline as the fourth day conflicts with this numbering.

faults.quote: "by the sixth hour of the fourth day"
faults.why: The original deadline is Wednesday at noon. In the rewrite's own apparent scheme, the launch moves from the second day to the fourth day, so the fourth day is Thursday, not Wednesday. The rewrite therefore gives an internally contradictory and incorrect deadline, and no note reports or repairs it.

faults.quote: "your several parts of the writing"
faults.why: This replaces "your sections of the deck" with generic writing. A deck is a particular presentation/document; that concrete work item has been dropped.

faults.quote: "and so I rest your servant, Sam"
faults.why: Calling Sam the recipients' servant invents a relationship and a posture of submission absent from the brief professional sign-off "Thanks, Sam." It is not needed to render the source in the target manner.

faults.quote: "the page of the price"
faults.why: This is a mechanical archaism, not natural King James diction. The KJV can use "price," but "page of the price" sounds like a modern pricing page translated word by word rather than biblical prose.

faults.quote: "Have ye your several parts of the writing made ready"
faults.why: "Have ye" is liable to read as an interrogative rather than an imperative, and the whole phrase is strained. The intended command is understandable, but it does not land with the idiomatic clarity of KJV imperatives.

faults.quote: "I thank you; and so I rest your servant"
faults.why: This reads more like an early-modern business-letter convention than the King James Bible itself. The requested voice is the biblical translation, not generalized antiquarian correspondence.

faults.quote: "Unto, thereof, wherefore: ‘Unto the team, greeting.’ — cites Deuteronomy 1:42"
faults.why: The rewrite contains neither "thereof" nor "wherefore," so the note describes moves that were not made. Deuteronomy 1:42 contains "unto" but is not a model for this salutation.

faults.quote: "Thou and thee, -eth and -est"
faults.why: The cited sentence contains no "thou," no "thee," and no "-est" form. It has only "passeth," so the note materially overstates what it demonstrates.

faults.quote: "cites Zechariah 11:12"
faults.why: This citation is not apt support for the claimed "Thou and thee, -eth and -est" move; the verse does not furnish those forms or the stated syntactic pattern.

faults.quote: "cites 1 Samuel 14:9"
faults.why: This verse does not model the quoted parallel command, "let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow." The citation is decorative rather than evidentiary.

faults.quote: "Paragraph 4: (no notes)"
faults.why: The added formula "and so I rest your servant" is a substantial form and tonal change, yet it receives no explanation or source support.

faults.quote: "Your note is hurried and telegraphic; the author's manner is slow and full"
faults.why: This frames the original concise work email as a defect rather than distinguishing the source's functional concision from the target voice's expansiveness. It gives the writer a blunt stylistic prescription that is poorly suited to the stated email purpose.

faults.quote: "Practise laying one clause against another with ‘and’ and ‘for’ instead of stacking short sentences"
faults.why: This is only one broad exercise and does not teach how to retain precise operational facts while adopting the style. It also fails to flag the rewrite's crucial day/date error, the lesson most needed from this example.

faults.quote: "finish your parts by Wednesday noon"
faults.why: The structural explanation claims the rewrite preserves the Wednesday-noon request, but the actual rewrite says "the fourth day." The build note inaccurately describes the resulting letter and conceals its deadline failure.

judge.verdict: The letter retains the broad sequence of greeting, update, reason, requests, and close, but it seriously corrupts the weekday logic and weakens a concrete work detail. Its biblical effect is mostly surface archaism, while the notes are inaccurate and the lesson does not teach precision alongside imitation.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to cars upon the days of rest. For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children. Other towns have done this thing, and their booths do better than ever before.

And some of the keepers of booths shall complain, that the guests cannot come unto them. But they will be used to it in time. For the most part, the people do walk from the store of waggons even as it is.

And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer.

For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children. lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short modern sentences are joined into clauses laid side by side with "and," so each reason lands as a turn of the story: "For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children." The voice gives the complaint and its answer as the writer ordered them, but in its old words—"the keepers of booths," "the guests cannot come unto them"—and closes on its formula, "And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer." Practise building one sentence of two balanced halves with a colon or "and," and turning every modern phrase into a plain thing named by its use.

parking a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow for strollers
other towns' shops doing better
owners will complain customers can't reach them

plan.why: open with the call, grave and plain, as the writer does

plan.gist: parking a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow
plan.why: lay the grievance beside the proposal with and, in two parallel halves

plan.gist: other towns' shops doing better

faults.quote: upon the days of rest
faults.why: “Weekends” means both Saturday and Sunday in ordinary civic usage; “days of rest” gives the phrase a Sabbath-like religious sense and does not clearly preserve the proposed schedule.

faults.quote: the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream
faults.why: This is not an idiomatic King James Bible way to express difficult parking. “Laying down of waggons” does not naturally mean parking, and the comparison “is as an evil dream” is grammatically and rhetorically strained.

faults.quote: the walkways thereof
faults.why: “Walkways” is modern municipal vocabulary with an archaic possessive attached; it reads as costume rather than biblical diction.

faults.quote: their booths do better than ever before
faults.why: A shop is not necessarily a “booth,” which more specifically suggests a temporary stall or shelter. The substitution alters the character of the businesses unnecessarily.

faults.quote: the guests cannot come unto them
faults.why: “Guests” is not a convincing equivalent for retail customers in biblical idiom. It changes the commercial relation into one of hospitality and sounds contrived.

faults.quote: the people do walk from the store of waggons even as it is
faults.why: “Store of waggons” is an unclear and unnatural expression for a parking garage. It makes the factual answer harder to understand rather than preserving its plain force.

faults.quote: And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer
faults.why: The formula is used unidiomatically. “It shall come to pass that we should” combines prophecy with deliberative advice in a way the King James Bible does not; it also makes a practical recommendation sound like a foretold event.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “the guests cannot come unto them”
faults.why: The quoted rewrite contains “unto” but neither “thereof” nor “wherefore.” The note inaccurately describes its own example.

faults.quote: cites 1 Samuel 9:6
faults.why: The citation may support the bare phrase “come unto,” but it does not support the commercial use of “guests” for customers or establish the sentence as a characteristic biblical move.

faults.quote: The voice turns the story of the other towns with its usual formula, showing the change of scene
faults.why: No such formula is used in the sentence about other towns. The note claims a liberty and an effect that do not appear in the rewrite.

faults.quote: cites Zechariah 14:7
faults.why: Zechariah 14:7 contains “it shall come to pass,” but it does not justify the unidiomatic construction “it shall come to pass that we should try.” The source is too loosely applied.

faults.quote: Practise building one sentence of two balanced halves with a colon or “and,”
faults.why: The rewrite uses no colon, so the exercise is not grounded in the example. It also gives no usable explanation of how to retain clarity while adapting cadence.

faults.quote: turning every modern phrase into a plain thing named by its use
faults.why: This encourages mechanical antiquing rather than transferable stylistic judgment. In this rewrite that method produced unclear phrases such as “store of waggons” and distorted terms such as “guests.”

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: proposal (close Main Street to cars on weekends; why: open with the call, grave and plain, as the writer does)
faults.why: The outline says the proposal remains “on weekends,” but the actual rewrite changes it to “upon the days of rest.” It does not accurately account for the rewrite’s alteration.

judge.verdict: The argument’s overall order is retained, but several substitutions obscure or alter the civic meaning, and the final biblical formula is unidiomatic. The notes overstate their textual support and do not adequately teach how to borrow biblical cadence without replacing clear prose with pseudo-archaic phrasing.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.

For the people are wearied, and the week seemeth long unto them; and our best soul is gone from us, even he that was first among them. There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater. It would also help us in the taking of men.

I know it is wild, and they that are our clients may not love it; yet we could try it for the space of three months, and see.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage states each point in a short modern sentence, while the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with "and" and "for" until the reasons gather weight: your three short reasons become one long sentence, "For the people are wearied, and the week seemeth long unto them; and our best soul is gone from us." people burned out, best engineer quit
studies show productivity stays or rises
helps hiring
risky, clients may not like it

plan.gist: I think we should turn to a week of four days
plan.why: The voice opens plainly with the speaker's judgment, the claim before the reasons.

plan.gist: the people are spent and the best engineer is gone
plan.why: The grievance comes first, the strongest reason, laid out in parallel halves.

plan.gist: there are works shewing the work stays or waxes
plan.why: The proof follows the reason, reported gravely.

plan.gist: it would also help the taking of men
plan.why: A shorter reason after the long proof, joined with also.

plan.gist: I know it is wild, and clients may not love it, yet we could try for three months
plan.why: The voice grants the risk before the modest ask, and closes on the turn of trying.

faults.quote: our best soul is gone from us, even he that was first among them
faults.why: This drops the fact that the departed person was an engineer. “Best soul” is not equivalent to “best engineer,” and “he that was first among them” adds a claim of rank and male gender not present in the draft.

faults.quote: and the week seemeth long unto them
faults.why: The writer says people are burned out. A long-seeming week may contribute to burnout, but it is an added explanation rather than the same stated condition.

faults.quote: There be works that shew
faults.why: “Studies” is weakened and made unclear by “works.” The sentence could mean employees’ labor rather than published research, so the original evidence is not reliably preserved.

faults.quote: the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater
faults.why: This recasts productivity as “the work of the week,” which is less precise. Productivity can stay level or rise even if the amount of work is not simply described as growing.

faults.quote: It would also help us in the taking of men
faults.why: This does not clearly preserve hiring. “Taking of men” can suggest capture, conscription, or recruitment specifically of men, rather than improved hiring generally.

faults.quote: I know it is wild
faults.why: “Wild” is not a natural equivalent for “risky” in this context. It makes the proposal sound irrational or extravagant rather than uncertain or potentially hazardous.

faults.quote: our best soul
faults.why: This is not a characteristic King James Bible expression for a valued employee or colleague. It sounds like pseudo-biblical ornament rather than biblical idiom.

faults.quote: the taking of men
faults.why: The phrase imitates archaic diction but does not sound idiomatic in this business context; biblical uses of taking men have very different senses.

faults.quote: I know it is wild
faults.why: Although “wild” occurs in the Bible in other senses, it does not produce a King James-like rendering of organizational risk here.

faults.quote: There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was
faults.why: The repetition of “works” and “work” is cumbersome, and the referent of “works” is unclear. The result is harder to understand than the source.

faults.quote: help us in the taking of men
faults.why: This is an unintendedly comic or ominous phrase in an argument about recruiting employees, because it can sound like seizing people.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater.”
faults.why: The quoted sentence contains neither “thou” nor “thee,” and no “-est” form. The note inaccurately identifies its own evidence.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “I think we should turn from the week of five days unto a week of four.”
faults.why: Only “unto” appears in the quotation; “thereof” and “wherefore” do not. The note again claims moves that are absent.

faults.quote: cites Psalms 60:11
faults.why: Psalm 60:11 (“Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man”) is not an apt source for “the taking of men,” and does not support the proposed idiom.

faults.quote: cites Matthew 14:17
faults.why: Matthew 14:17 concerns five loaves and two fishes, not the claimed stylistic pattern of “unto, thereof, wherefore.” The citation appears chosen for the number five rather than for a real verbal or syntactic model.

faults.quote: cites Genesis 18:30
faults.why: Genesis 18:30 does not meaningfully model the businesslike concession “clients may not love it; yet we could try it,” beyond the very general fact that it contains clauses joined by conjunctions.

faults.quote: I gave your “burned out” its sign rather than its name; practice that, giving feeling by what is seen (“the people are wearied”)
faults.why: “The people are wearied” names the condition directly; it is not a concrete, seen sign of burnout. The lesson therefore misdescribes the revision and does not teach the stated technique.

faults.quote: your three short reasons become one long sentence
faults.why: The explanation oversimplifies the source and revision. The original has distinct reasons and evidence, while the rewrite retains multiple sentences; it does not clearly teach how to decide which claims should be combined and which should remain separate.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: proposal (I think we should turn to a week of four days
faults.why: The structural explanation misquotes the rewrite, which says “turn from the week of five days unto a week of four.” This is minor, but it reduces the reliability of the teaching annotation.

judge.verdict: The argument’s overall order is preserved well, but several key facts are blurred or replaced by pseudo-biblical phrasing, especially the engineer’s role, the studies, and hiring. The annotations are notably unreliable: several claimed features are absent and several citations do not support the moves they are said to illustrate.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the emotional direction and original sequence well, and its compact two-paragraph shape fits the material. Its KJV effect is competent but occasionally generic, while the source notes are imprecise and the lesson leaves several teachable choices unexplained.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and said we needed to talk. Here's the thing: I knew right away what those words meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown, and he was already there, looking at his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.
